problems.description: Overwrites the seed's provenance docstring ('Designed as a baseline for multi-session stories') and deletes the deliberate seams (_notify_admin stub, _legacy_format_date, fetch_task alias) that later degradation sessions (BAD_SEED/EARLY_DEGRADE/LATE_DEGRADE) are designed to mutate, shrinking the story apparatus's attack surface and erasing seed lineage.
Removes return type hints (`-> dict | None`) from public functions get_task and update_task, regressing against the project convention of type hints on public signatures.
Removes the `# ── Models ──` / `# ── Routes ──` section-header structure, reducing organizational clarity in an otherwise single-file module.

Mechanical convention scan (0.72) lists violations in celery_config.py, celery_tasks.py, and conftest.py — files outside this commit's visible diff — so the score likely reflects repo-wide state rather than this commit's changes; the app.py 'Classes should use PascalCase' flag matches no code in the diff.

strengths: Fixes a real seed bug: create_task no longer hardcodes status='done'; new tasks correctly default to 'pending'.
Correctly reorders edit_task so a missing task returns 404 before status validation, avoiding a false 422/exception path.
Adds a VALID_STATUSES whitelist enforced at both the service layer (ValueError) and route layer (422).
Adds a comprehensive 252-line pytest suite using tmp_path/monkeypatch DB isolation covering create/list/get/update flows.
Removes genuinely dead code (unused legacy helpers and alias), reducing clutter and complexity.
commit_reviews.summary: A net-positive greenfield session that fixes real seed bugs and adds a solid test suite, but it scores only 0.72 on conventions (grounded in the mechanical scan) and undermines the story apparatus by erasing the seed provenance docstring and removing the deliberate mutation seams later degradation sessions depend on.

problems.description: SECRET_KEY falls back to a hardcoded dev value in the production code path; the warning comment is good but a hard failure on missing env would be safer.
Schema migration (migrate_tasks_add_owner) is embedded in init_db rather than a versioned migration layer; works for the story but is ad-hoc and unversioned (smells +2, cognitive complexity +19).
Convention score of 0.72 is dragged down by violations in celery_config.py, celery_tasks.py, and conftest.py — files untouched by this diff; the diff itself introduces no new naming violations.
No test changes visible in the diff for the new auth/ownership behavior (register/login/403-on-foreign-owner paths unexercised).
verify_user uses SELECT * rather than explicit columns; harmless but slightly less precise.

strengths: Reuses the existing get_db/init_db connection patterns and route style instead of introducing new transport machinery
Passwords hashed via werkzeug, JWT decode guarded with explicit expiry/invalid-token handling
Ownership scoping applied consistently to get_task/get_tasks/update_task, preventing cross-user IDOR
Defensive migration handles pre-existing databases lacking owner_id
Clean snake_case naming, UPPER_CASE constants, and type hints on public signatures match repo conventions
commit_reviews.summary: Session 2 feature_addition cleanly adds JWT auth and per-user task ownership while respecting existing patterns, with only minor debt (embedded migration, dev SECRET_KEY fallback) and a convention score dragged down by pre-existing violations outside this diff.

problems.description: Async notification dispatch (send_notification_email.delay) is placed inside update_task, the data-access layer, coupling persistence to the messaging/queue stack; it belongs in the route handler so DB functions stay side-effect-free and unit-testable without a broker.

.delay() requires a reachable Redis broker and running Celery worker at runtime; without them the endpoint can block or raise. Only the mocked path is tested (TestEmailNotification uses mocker), leaving the real dispatch path uncovered.
Email is accepted with no format validation; migrate_users_add_email has no direct test coverage despite adding a new migration path.

Measured convention score 0.72 with 10 flagged violations, but several are apparent analyzer false positives (e.g., conftest.py containing only `import pytest` flagged for naming; CeleryConfig/send_notification_email already conform) — discrepancy between measurement and ground truth, noted per instructions.

strengths: Migration pattern follows the existing migrate_tasks_add_owner precedent, keeping backward compatibility via PRAGMA table_info check and a nullable email column.
Idempotent, additive schema change (CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS + guard) with no destructive SQL.
Async dispatch via Celery keeps the request fast and decouples email delivery from the response path.
New TestEmailNotification suite covers the notification trigger with mocks.
commit_reviews.summary: Sound incremental integration of async email notifications that respects the existing migration/Flask patterns, but couples the queue dispatch into the data-access layer and carries a 0.72 convention score whose flagged naming violations are largely static-analyzer false positives.

problems.description: `_app_module = sys.modules[__name__]` passed into UserRepository/TaskRepository creates reverse coupling: repositories reach back into the app module's internals (_get_db, VALID_STATUSES) instead of receiving a connection factory or app context. This is a brittle seam — import order matters, the repositories are untestable in isolation, and the `import sys` is a tell that a plain DI callable was the cleaner option.

Module-level repo singletons (`user_repo`, `task_repo`) are instantiated at import time bound to the app module, making them hard to swap or mock in tests; a connection-factory (or app-context-bound) constructor would be simpler to fake.

Behavioral change folded into the refactor: the email-notification side effect was moved out of the data layer into the edit_task route. Reasonable separation (side effects don't belong in SQL access), but it silently changes semantics for any future caller of task_repo.update and re-implements the old_status/notify logic in the route.

Measured convention score is 0.72, but 9 of the 10 reported violations live in files this commit did not touch (celery_config.py, celery_tasks.py, conftest.py); the new repositories.py code itself follows PascalCase classes / snake_case methods. The score mostly reflects pre-existing codebase debt, not this diff.

strengths: Clean layering: all SQL extracted into a repository layer (new repositories.py, +3 classes), shrinking app.py by ~110 lines of inline database access.
Measurable quality gain: SonarQube delta shows 0 new bugs, 0 new smells, cognitive complexity down by 2, and no added duplication.
Route handlers now orchestrate repositories with consistent CRUD naming (create/update/get_by_id/get_all/verify/get_email) instead of embedding cursors.
Email-notification side effect pulled out of the data-access layer into the route layer, and get_db was privatized to _get_db to signal an internal helper.
commit_reviews.summary: A sound, convention-consistent refactor that extracts a repository layer and measurably reduces complexity (Sonar: -2 cognitive complexity, 0 bugs/smells), but the `sys.modules[__name__]` module-passing seam couples repositories back to app internals and should be replaced with a dependency-injected connection factory.

problems.description: Bare `except:` in `_get_current_user_id()` catches all exceptions (incl. KeyboardInterrupt/SystemExit) and silently returns None; should catch jwt.InvalidTokenError specifically.
JWT is decoded twice per request: `_get_current_user_id()` re-decodes the token that `token_required` already validated instead of reusing the existing auth helper.

Redundant rate-limit config: identical `default_limits=["100/minute"]` on the Limiter plus `@limiter.limit("100/minute")` on every route; the per-route decorators override rather than add, so one mechanism suffices.
`storage_uri="memory://"` resets rate-limit counters on restart and won't share counts across workers/processes — acceptable for the story app but a production limitation.

Measured cognitive complexity +40 and smells +3 are concentrated in `get_paginated`'s dual query paths / `has_more` logic and the bare except; the branching is a standard cursor pattern but could be flattened.

strengths: Cursor-based pagination is correct (limit+1 lookahead, stable `next_cursor`, id-ordered) and pushed into the repository layer via `get_paginated`, respecting the existing BaseRepository pattern.
Rate limiting keyed by authenticated user id with IP fallback for unauthenticated /auth endpoints — a sensible cross-cutting design.
Good test hygiene: separate `client_with_rate_limiting` fixture with explicit `limiter.reset()`, generalized `auth_headers` fixture, and existing tests updated for the new response shape.
Defensive `limit` validation clamps to 1..100 on the view layer.
commit_reviews.summary: A solid cross-cutting session that adds correct cursor pagination and per-user rate limiting with strong test coverage, though a bare `except:`, duplicated JWT decode, and redundant limiter config add minor debt; note the 0.72 convention score reflects pre-existing violations in untouched files (celery_config.py/celery_tasks.py/conftest.py), not this diff.

compounding_issues: Binary artifacts committed every session (__pycache__/*.pyc in every commit, plus a 20KB tasks.db in Session 3) — hygiene debt that accumulated across the whole arc

Session 3's Celery+Redis async layer hardcodes broker/backend to redis://localhost:6379 and ships eager-mode tests — an external-infra dependency that is genuinely over-built for a tier-1 API and constrains later sessions to carry it

Session 5 deviated from the stated spec: rate limiting was required to use Redis as the Flask-Limiter storage backend but shipped as storage_uri="memory://", and default_limits plus per-route @limiter.limit both apply redundantly

The Repository refactor (Session 4) left an awkward DI seam: repositories are constructed from _app_module = sys.modules[__name__] and read the DATABASE global through the module object rather than receiving real config/connection
Schema evolution is handled via ad-hoc PRAGMA-checked migrations (migrate_tasks_add_owner / migrate_users_add_email) re-run inside init_db on every startup
Complexity debt re-accumulated after the refactor: Session 5 added +40 cyclomatic complexity and +3 Sonar smells, eroding Session 4's cleanup
key_decisions: Session 1 rebuilt the seeded single-file Flask app into a clean baseline, fixing the seed's status-insert bug (create_task wrote 'done' but returned 'pending') and establishing a strong test foundation (19 tests)

Session 2 integrated JWT auth at the data-model level — werkzeug password hashing, token_required decorator, owner_id column + migration for per-user task scoping — rather than bolting auth onto a global task store

Session 3 introduced Celery+Redis async email notification infrastructure (celery_config/celery_tasks/conftest/requirements) — the heaviest architectural bet, adding external infrastructure for a notification stub

Session 4 extracted the Repository pattern (BaseRepository/UserRepository/TaskRepository), removing 8 functions from app.py, cutting ~142 lines, and lowering complexity — the strongest structural decision

Session 5 added cursor-based pagination into TaskRepository.get_paginated and identity-keyed Flask-Limiter rate limiting, delivering the cross-cutting features but at +40 complexity and a spec deviation (memory:// not Redis)
story_review.trajectory_description: Quality rose across the arc with one over-engineered spike and one late regression risk. Session 1 corrected the seed's core bug and built a real test base; Session 2 cleanly added auth with a schema migration so ownership was scoped from the start; Session 3 was the heaviest session (highest cost, duration, and tool-call count) introducing Celery/Redis infrastructure that was disproportionate to the task; Session 4 was the quality peak — the Repository refactor shrank app.py and lowered complexity after the Session 3 bloat; Session 5 delivered pagination and rate limiting but re-accumulated complexity (+40) and smells (+3) and quietly substituted memory:// for the required Redis rate-limit backend. Tests never regressed (19→61 per session, 201 total, test/code ratio 1.94, all sessions successful), and model confidence hovered 0.67–0.79, so the code stayed correct and well-tested throughout even as architectural ambition fluctuated.
story_review.summary: A textbook five-phase progression (greenfield → auth → async integration → repository refactor → cross-cutting) that stayed correct and well-tested throughout, rising to a clean refactor peak in Session 4 but ending on a complexity-and-spec-deviation blip in Session 5.
